Commercial Roofers in Bird in Hand

A practical commercial roofing plan for Bird in Hand properties separates urgent leak control from repair, coating, maintenance, and replacement decisions supported by photos and condition findings. Bird-in-Hand runs on tourism traffic built on its smorgasbord restaurants, the farmers market, and a cluster of inns and bed-and-breakfast lodging. Each of those building types puts a different set of demands on a roof, and none of them can afford to close during the season the roof needs work done.

Large-Span Roofs Over Banquet and Buffet Halls

The smorgasbord restaurants here run large clear-span dining and banquet rooms with commercial kitchens attached, and the roof over that kitchen section works harder than the rest of the building. Grease-laden exhaust, multiple rooftop units, and heavy foot traffic from kitchen staff accessing equipment all concentrate wear around the same penetrations.

We detail those exhaust curbs and equipment pads to keep grease and heat from breaking down the membrane early, and we build in walk pads on routes staff actually use, not only where a drawing says they should.

The Farmers Market Building and Retail Stalls

The farmers market building is a different roofing problem: a long open span over stalls selling produce, meats, baked goods, and quilts, with humidity and temperature swings from the market floor below affecting the deck from underneath as much as weather affects it from above. Leaks over food stalls create a faster, more expensive problem than a leak over a storage room.

Coordinating any roof work with the market's operating schedule — usually closed certain days of the week — lets us get access without disrupting vendors during business hours.

Inns, Guest Lodging, and Steep-Slope Sections

Bird-in-Hand's inns and B&B lodging mix pitched, shingled roofs on the original structure with flat or low-slope additions built on later for extra rooms, meeting space, or a breakfast room. That mix means two different systems on one property, sometimes meeting at a valley or a step-flashed wall that's a common source of leaks if it wasn't detailed correctly originally.

  • Asphalt or architectural shingle on original inn structures
  • TPO or EPDM over flat rear additions and meeting rooms
  • Standing seam metal on some newer lodging additions
  • Membrane roofs over attached banquet and event space
  • Built-up or modified bitumen on older market and retail buildings

Scheduling Reroofing Around Peak Tourist Months

Spring through fall is when Bird-in-Hand sees the most visitor traffic, and a reroof or major repair during that window is disruptive for a business whose parking lot and dining room are full most days. We plan larger jobs for the shoulder season when we can, and where a summer repair can't wait, we sequence the work to keep at least one dining or lodging section open.

Motorcoach parking areas often have canopy or shelter structures of their own, and those get scheduled around tour bus arrival times rather than blocking access during peak hours.

Coating and Recover Options for Older Membrane

A lot of the flat-roof sections on Bird-in-Hand's restaurant and lodging buildings are older membrane that's still structurally sound but showing UV wear and seam fatigue. A silicone coating or a recover layer over the existing roof can extend its life significantly at a fraction of tear-off cost, which matters for a seasonal business managing cash flow around its busiest months.

We inspect the existing roof first to confirm it's a good coating or recover candidate before recommending it over a full replacement, since a coating applied to a membrane that's already past its useful life just delays a necessary replacement without solving the underlying problem.

Where a coating makes sense, it also gives an owner a lighter-color reflective surface that helps with rooftop unit efficiency during the humid Lancaster County summers, a secondary benefit worth factoring into the decision alongside the direct cost savings over tear-off.

Roof Inspections Ahead of Peak Season

The best time to find a small leak or a worn flashing detail on a Bird-in-Hand property is before the parking lot fills up for the season, not after a wet spring weekend when a dining room ceiling starts staining. We recommend a pre-season inspection in early spring for restaurants, markets, and lodging buildings, walking every roof section and checking drains, seams, and penetrations while there's still time to schedule repairs without disrupting business.

That inspection also gives an owner a realistic read on how many seasons a roof has left, which matters for budgeting a reroof around a slower year rather than being forced into an emergency project during peak traffic.

For properties with several buildings on one site — a main restaurant, a gift shop, and a lodging wing, for example — we inspect all of them on the same visit and give a single prioritized report rather than treating each building as a separate call.

What Bird-in-Hand Property Owners Ask Us

Can reroofing happen without closing during the season?

Usually yes, by sequencing the work in sections and scheduling around your dining and lodging hours. Full closures are rare and only necessary for a complete tear-off on a small building.

Do smorgasbord kitchens need special roof detailing?

Yes. Exhaust curbs, grease exposure, and heavy rooftop equipment traffic all need to be detailed for durability, not only standard flashing.

How do you handle inn roofs that mix shingle and flat sections?

We treat each section as its own system and pay particular attention to where they meet, since that transition is usually where leaks start on a mixed roof.

What about motorcoach canopy and shelter structures?

Those get inspected and maintained on the same schedule as the main building roof, with work timed around tour bus arrivals.

Is a coating or recover a realistic option instead of full replacement?

Often, if the existing membrane is still sound. We inspect first and only recommend a coating or recover when the roof is a genuine candidate for it.
